While we can thank Aristotle for noting the birds ingenuity, this particular behavior has not been otherwise observed.

name: Oriole
description: Sightly songbirds with yellow and black plumage, the common name oriole applies to two unrelated groups of birds Icteridae, found in the Americas, and Oriolidae, found in Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia. Esteemed for its music, the black naped oriole appeared on decorative badges, called mandarin squares, of high ranking court officials in China during the Ming dynasty 1368 1644. In the 1760s, during the Qing dynasty, they were adopted as the symbol for court musicians.

name: Osprey
description: A large raptor whose name derives from the Latin ossifraga, meaning bone breaker, the osprey appears in various myths and legends, often as a ferocious predator. The birds impressive fishing skills were recorded by a thirteenth century Dominican friar and Doctor of the Church, Albertus Magnus, who believed the osprey had one webbed foot for swimming and one sharply clawed talon for catching prey. Although this is not factual, the bird does have large hooked talons and barbs on the pads of its feet, perfect for capturing slippery fish.

name: Ostrich
description: The largest, heaviest, and fastest running land bird on Earth, the ostrich cannot fly but is noted for its legendary strength. So impressed was Pliny the Elder by these mammoth birds that he claimed they could eat every substance without distinction. Many more legends developed, including a medieval myth describing the birds ability to hatch its eggs by staring at them intently. Even more storied than the ostrich, however, are its massive eggs, the yolks of which are equivalent in terms of size and nutrition to that of about twenty four chicken eggs. As early as 4000 BCE, ostrich eggs were hollowed out, occasionally carved with intricate designs, and used as perfume containers and drinking cups. In ancient Egypt, the eggs fed pharaohs and were included in funeral rites, and in ancient Greece and Rome, they were offered to deities.

name: Owl
description: Nocturnal birds with haunting cries, owls are regarded as harbingers of evil and even death in many cultures. Chaucer noted this in The Parliament of Fowls, stating, The owl too, that portent of death does bring. Shakespeare echoed the sentiment in Henry VI, Part 3 The owl shrieked at thy birth, an evil sign. But the association of owls with ill omens isnt exclusively Western; the Kikuyu people of Kenya believe the birds call warns of impending death. Owls have often been associated with witchcraft. For example, the ancient Romans believed that the Strix or Striges were witches who could transform into owl like creatures to feed on human blood. The order Strigiformes takes its name from these malevolent beasts.

name: Parakeet
description: The long tailed parakeet is an attractive bird with green, red, and blue plumage. In a folktale from northern Sumatra, Indonesia, a group of parakeets is captured by a hunter. The king of the parakeets convinces his flock to play dead so that the hunter will release them. The ruse works, and all of the parakeets manage to escape except for the king, who is taken to a palace and enclosed in a golden cage. The parakeet king is devastated, but he hatches another plan he stops eating, stops singing, and pretends to be seriously ill to convince his captors he is dying. When his cage is opened, he flies out and is reunited with his flock.

name: Parrot
description: Large and exceptionally colorful birds, parrots have long captured the human imagination. According to a South Asian legend, the Buddha was once born as a small gray parrot. When a storm sparked a wildfire in his forest, the parrot began dipping himself in the river and desperately shaking his wings over the flames. Seeing this, a god of the heavens was moved by the little parrots efforts to save the forest. The god wept, and his tears extinguished the blaze. Charred by flames and doused in tears, the once homely parrot became an exquisite, brightly colored bird red for the fire, blue for the water, green for the forest, and yellow for the sun.

name: Peacock
description: The peacock, unlike the modest female peahen, is a showy and stately bird revered as sacred in a number of cultures.; In the Middle Eastern Yazidi religion, Taws Melek Kurdish for Peacock Angel is the leader of Gods seven angels. He is responsible for all that occurs in nature the earth, sky, mountains, and sea.; In ancient Greece, the peacock was sacred to Hera and pulled the goddesss chariot. The ancient Greeks, who believed peacocks did not decay after death, associated these birds with immortality.; The Sanskrit word for peacock mayura is associated with many Hindu gods; the peacock is also the national bird of India, which is its home country. In one legend, Indra, the Hindu god of rain, was fighting the demon Ravana when a peacock shielded him by hiding him from view. To thank the bird, Indra gave him beautiful blue green feathers.

name: Pelican
description: The fascinating lore of these water birds can be traced to the Physiologus, an educational Christian text compiled in the third century by an unknown Greek author. It states that pelicans kill their young in frustration, then revive them in their remorse using their own blood, an allegory for the resurrection of Jesus. This was likely a misunderstanding of how pelicans feed their young they regurgitate food from the red pouch under their bill, pressing the pouch against their chest to empty it completely. The result is a bloody looking mess.; Medieval Christians modified this understanding, believing that, in her intense devotion, the pelican mother would wound her breast to feed her young with her own blood. Queen Elizabeth I of England even adopted this symbolism; in a famous portrait by Nicholas Hilliard, she wears a pelican pendant on her chest.

name: Penguin
description: Penguins, with their distinguished black and white feathers and upright posture, are noted for their friendly demeanor; the birds generally have no fear of humans.; The Maori people call the Fiordland penguin tawaki, named for a god who once walked the earth as a human.; The people did not realize Tawaki was a god until he threw off his garb and dressed himself in lightning, revealing his true nature to humankind. The feathered crest of the Fiordland penguin does indeed resemble lightning.

name: Peregrine falcon
description: The word peregrine, from the Latin peregrinus, means wanderer or traveler, and the peregrine falcon also called simply the peregrine is associated with a number of deities who undertook sacred journeys. The Norse goddess Freyja was said to wear a cloak of falcon feathers as she traveled between worlds. The ancient Egyptian gods Khonsu and Horus are both depicted as falcon headed men Khonsu, whose name also means traveler or wanderer, was the god of the moon, perceived to travel across the sky each night. Similarly, the sky god Horus was thought to contain both the sun and the moon; as he traversed the sky in his falcon form, so too would the sun his right eye and the moon, his left.

name: Petrel
description: Named for Saint Peter, these birds fly close to the waters surface as they look for food, appearing to walk on water as Peter did, briefly, in the Gospel of Matthew.; Eighteenth century British sailors believed petrels to be harbingers of storms, calling them Mother Careys chickens. Related to the mythic Davy Jones, Mother Carey was a supernatural embodiment of the cruelty of the sea.

name: Pheasant
description: Like peacocks, male pheasants are more brightly colored than their female counterparts. In China, the golden pheasant is one of the inspirations behind the f ng huang, a mythical bird similar to the phoenix.; It appears in both ancient and modern Chinese jewelry, wedding decorations, home decor, and artwork. An immortal bird, it is associated with peace and prosperity.

name: Phoebe
description: The phoebe is a small, gray colored flycatcher named for the sound of its call fee bee. Taking the Greek spelling, the name also recalls Phoebe, the mythic Titaness who was the daughter of Uranus and Gaia the Sky and the Earth and grandmother to Apollo, Artemis, and Hecate.; The original owner of the site of the Oracle of Delphi, Phoebe was associated with prophetic insight. Her name, meaning bright, was later adapted into a forename for Apollo, the sun god, and an alternative name for Artemis, goddess of the moon.

name: Pigeon
description: Pigeons were domesticated about five thousand years ago and have a unique homing ability, meaning they instinctively return to their nests even after traveling long distances away. For this reason, they were relied upon to deliver messages in ancient Egypt and by the Mongol emperor Genghis Khan.; More recently, they have carried postal messages and wartime communications.; One homing pigeon, Cher Ami, was wounded in battle during the First World War and received honors for managing to deliver a message despite his injuries. During the Second World War, Paddy, an Irish carrier pigeon, received the Dickin Medal for being the first pigeon to arrive in England with news of the successful D Day invasion. The heroic bird flew over 230 miles across the English Channel in just under five hours.

name: Plover
description: Sometimes mistaken for lapwings, plovers are wading birds found around the world. The golden plover in particular holds a special place in the folklore of Iceland. In this far northern country, the sight of the first golden plover indicates the arrival of spring.; The birds melancholic calls are said to sing away the snow, reminding Icelanders that the respite of warmer days is ahead.

name: Potoo
description: The potoo is a fascinating nocturnal bird with cryptic plumage that allows it to blend in with stumps and branches. Native to Central and South America, this elusive bird with large, dark eyes has a ghostly quality. The Shuar people of Ecuador and Peru believe that the moon comes out when it hears the haunting cry of the potoo.; According to legend, a man angry with his wife fled to the sky and became the moon; his wife became the potoo, grieving for him at night.

name: Prairie chicken
description: The prairie chicken is a type of grouse found across the North American prairies. Its scientific name, Tympanuchus, comes from the Greek for holding a drum and refers to the birds neck sack, which helps produce its booming call.; Both the Blackfoot and Cree peoples have honored the bird for centuries by performing the Prairie Chicken Dance, imitating the beautiful, elaborate mating dance of the male prairie chicken.

name: Puffin
description: A black and white seabird with a vibrant orange bill, the stocky puffin is a striking sight to behold on rocky coastal cliffs. Its scientific name, Fratercula, comes from the Latin fraterculus, meaning little brother, likely because the birds plumage resembles the robe of a monk.; In Ireland, where some believe these sacred birds bear the reincarnated souls of dead friars, the modest, hardworking puffin can be found fishing in turbulent seas or walking with a bowed head along a craggy shore.

name: Quail
description: Ground nesting birds more likely to be heard than seen, quails are often hunted and eaten as game. In Greek mythology, Asteria, the Titaness and daughter of Phoebe, avoided Zeuss advances by turning herself into a quail and diving into the sea, where she became the island of Delos.; When Asterias sister, Leto, was impregnated by Zeus, she avoided Heras jealous rage by taking refuge on Delos, where she gave birth to her twins, Artemis and Apollo.

name: Quetzal
description: A small bird with emerald green feathers, the tropical quetzal is found in the forests of Central and South America. Revered by the Aztecs and Maya, the quetzal was associated with the feathered serpent god, Quetzalc atl, and symbolized goodness, light, wealth, and freedom.; Although rulers and other nobles traditionally wore the feathers of the quetzal, they were careful not to harm the sacred bird while harvesting its plumes. Killing the quetzal was an offense punishable by death.

name: Raven
description: With jet black feathers and a massive wingspan, the ravens imposing size, keen intelligence, and dark coloring set it apart from all other birds.; In Norse mythology, two ravens called Huginn and Muninn sit atop the shoulders of the one eyed god Odin. His companions and his spies, the birds fly around the world each day and report back to their master, whispering their findings in his ear.; The ravens association with Odin, considered the father of the Norse gods, suggests an immense respect for the birds wisdom, but it also acknowledges its role as a scavenger. Like Odin, the god of war, the raven could be ruthless, circling over battlefields scavenging for prey.

name: Rhea
description: Distant relative of the ostrich and emu, this large flightless bird is named for the ancient Greek Titaness Rhea, mother of Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Hestia, Demeter, and Hades. Rhea may derive from the Greek ra, meaning ground or earth, a suitable name for a land bound bird.

name: Roadrunner
description: The roadrunner, also called the chaparral, is a fast running bird capable of accelerating up to twenty six miles per hour. Like the cartoon character of the same name, the bird is notoriously difficult to catch. Apart from its speed, its unique toe anatomy creates X shaped footprints that could lead in any direction. For this reason, the Pueblo people of the American Southwest re create the roadrunners footprints outside the tents of their deceased, hoping to confuse evil spirits and prevent them from following the souls of the dead.

name: Rooster
description: An adult male chicken is larger than the female of the species, with more brightly colored feathers and a larger red comb atop his head. Known to crow in anticipation of the dawn, the rooster and his call have come to signify daybreak.; Though his sunrise greeting lends the rooster a mostly cheerful reputation, the bird is also associated with betrayal. All four canonical Gospels tell of Jesus prediction at the Last Supper that his disciple Peter would betray him three times before the rooster crows. Indeed, Peter did deny Jesus in the lead up to his crucifixion. In the ninth century, Pope Nicholas I decreed that a rooster be placed atop every church in Europe as a reminder of this betrayal. Because weather vanes were already present on many church steeples, roosters were added to the devices, creating the now ubiquitous weathercock. The oldest surviving weathercock, the Gallo di Ramperto, was installed around the year 820 atop the bell tower of a church in Brescia, Italy.

name: Shrike
description: Shrikes are notoriously brutal predators, impaling their victims on sharp sticks, barbed wire, and thorns. Often called butcherbirds, they ensnare large insects, like crickets and grasshoppers, as well as mice, lizards, frogs, and even small birds. Despite their small stature only about nine inches they manage to hunt like much larger raptors. Old folk names for the shrike, such as wariangle or w rgengel, translate to choking angel and hint at the birds deceptively sweet appearance.

name: Snipe
description: Snipes, which share a family with curlews and sandpipers, are coastal waders with notably narrow bills. According to an old Chinese proverb, in the fight between the snipe and the clam, the fisherman has the best of it. In the fable, a snipe pecked at an open clam, which in turn closed its shell on the birds bill. Neither party would yield, so a passing fisherman netted them both and had them for dinner.

name: Sparrow
description: Petite birds that thrive in both urban and rural habitats, sparrows tend to be associated with sexuality. In ancient Greece, the sparrow was a symbol of Aphrodite, goddess of love. Over the centuries, however, its image became more lustful than loving. In The Canterbury Tales, Chaucer described the sparrow as hot and lecherous. At that time in Britain, sparrow pie believed to be an aphrodisiac was a common dish. Because the birds were so populous, they were easily captured from the eaves of houses using specially made sparrow pots.

name: Starling
description: A gifted mimic, the starling gets its name from the way its wings make it look like a star overhead.; A starling appears in the Mabinogion, an ancient collection of Welsh folklore, in the story of siblings Branwen and Br n. Branwen, sister of the king of Britain, marries Matholwch, the king of Ireland, and is taken from Wales to live in his country. She is treated cruelly by her new husband but manages to tame a starling and teach it to speak and sends the bird across the sea to her brother Br n to tell him of her strife. When he receives the message, Br n brings his army from Wales to rescue his sister.; While the Welsh myth may seem far fetched, a historical starling was the beloved pet of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. Reportedly, the bird could sing part of Mozarts Piano Concerto no. 17 in G Major. When the starling died just three years after its adoption, the famous composer held an elaborate funeral for his cherished companion and muse.

name: Stonechat
description: The stonechats call sounds a bit like two pebbles knocking against one another, hence the name stonechat. Scottish folklore claims that the stonechat is the devils bird, often chatting with Satan himself. Another Scottish tale suggests that toads help incubate the eggs of the stonechat. Both creatures were seen as strange and were associated with ill omens.

name: Stork
description: Large, long legged wading birds, storks are commonly associated with the arrival of new babies. The origins of this folklore are unclear, but versions of the myth appear across Europe, the Americas, and the Middle East. In Slavic mythology, storks carried unborn souls from Iriy, an otherworldly paradise, to Earth in the springtime.; The birds association with family may date to the Lex Ciconaria, or stork law, of ancient Rome, which required citizens to care for their elderly parents. The laws name drew on a belief among Romans that storks took great care of their families, particularly their elders. Younger storks were even thought to carry their parents on their backs when they became too feeble to fly.

name: Swallow
description: The swallow family consists of agile and attractive birds found around the world. Prior to the nineteenth century, European scholars obsessed over where these birds went in the winter. Aristotle suggested that some hibernated; the sixteenth century Swedish cartographer Olaus Magnus believed they wintered in the mud underwater; and, most outlandishly, the English minister and professor Charles Morton claimed they voyaged to the moon. Eventually, it was discovered that the birds flew as far as South Africa.; Perhaps due to Magnuss theory, sailors began to associate swallows with a safe return. Since the birds were often sighted close to land, spotting one at sea meant the shore was near. Sailor tattoos dating back to the sixteenth century often featured swallows. A swallow on one side of the chest indicated that a sailor had traveled five thousand nautical miles; a second swallow on the opposite side meant hed sailed twice as far.

name: Swan
description: Elegant, alluring white birds, swans have inspired a number of myths, many of which describe swans that transform into humans, or humans who become swans. In one such tale from Ireland called the Children of Lir, a jealous stepmother turned her four stepchildren into swans. They lived for nine hundred years and were revered for their enchanting songs and poems.; Perhaps most famous of all swan tales is Tchaikovskys Swan Lake. The ballet features Odette, a princess transformed into the titular bird by an evil sorcerer, Baron von Rothbart. Odette can only take a human form between midnight and daybreak, which is when Prince Siegfried falls in love with her. The sorcerer tricks Siegfried into professing his love, not for Odette but for Rothbarts daughter, Odile. When Siegfried realizes his mistake, he finds Odette, who is cursed to remain a swan forever. The two throw themselves into the lake, and their love breaks the curse.

name: Swift
description: The swift is associated with constant motion. Commonly confused for swallows, some swifts can spend up to ten months flying nonstop. Because the birds short legs are adapted for clinging to vertical surfaces, like trees or chimneys, it is rarely seen landing on the ground. It was even once thought to be footless, a quality reflected in its scientific name, apus, from the Greek for without feet.; The swift is believed to be the inspiration behind the heraldic symbol of the martlet, which often represented a fourth son. Due to the law of primogeniture, which originated in medieval Europe and lasted into the twentieth century, fourth sons had no land inheritance and were seen as wanderers much like the restless swift.

name: Thrasher
description: Named for the noisy way it thrashes about on the ground foraging for food, the thrasher is a noted vocalist and close relative of the catbird and mockingbird. An individual thrasher knows between one thousand and three thousand song phrases, the largest documented repertoire of any bird. Due to its two sided syrinx, or vocal organ, this bird can sing two harmonious tones at once, producing a truly unique sound.

name: Thrush
description: Known for its ethereal song, the thrush plays an important role in a legend told by the Oneida people of North America Long ago, as the Creator walked through the forests, he realized that birds made no sound. To remedy this, he held a competition to award the birds with individual songs. Each bird would fly as far as it could into the sky, and when it could fly no farther, it would find its song. The bird who flew the farthest would receive the most beautiful song of all. Desiring to win the competition, the thrush hid himself on the back of the eagle, who he was sure would fly the farthest. Once the eagle had flown as far as he could go, the thrush took off, flying even farther into the sky. There, he heard a beautiful song, which he learned to sing before flying back to the earth. When he returned, the other birds were displeased with him, and the thrush felt ashamed of his actions. He chose to hide away in the woods, where he is rarely seen, but he can still be heard singing his enchanting song.

name: Titmouse
description: Small and noisy, titmice are closely related to chickadees and play a role in the Cherokee legend of Spearfinger, in which an honest chickadee helps the villagers vanquish an evil witch. Before the chickadee can help, the arrogant titmouse misleads the villagers by telling them to aim their arrows at the witchs heart. But the arrows they shoot bounce off Spearfingers chest and are broken. Revealed to be a liar, the titmouse is captured, and its tongue is cut off as punishment.

name: Toucan
description: Magnificent birds with contrasting plumage and brightly colored bills, toucans are revered by Indigenous peoples in Central and South America, where their feathers often feature in ceremonial headdresses.; Myths about the toucan frequently focus on its beak, which, in addition to being vibrant, is one third the length of the birds body. A Brazilian folktale claims that the toucan became king of the birds by perching inside a hole in a tree, displaying his bill but hiding his body. The other birds accepted him as king, believing such an impressive beak could only belong to a massive bird. When the king finally emerged from his hole, however, he was mocked for his unusual proportions.

name: Turkey
description: In the United States, the turkey is primarily a symbol of the Thanksgiving holiday, associated with hearty nourishment. However, long before the American holiday developed, these birds were revered by the ancient Maya. The bones of the domestic turkey have been found at the Jaguar Paw Temple in modern day Guatemala, far from the birds natural habitat, indicating it was transported across long distances, likely for rituals and ceremonies. Images of the turkey native to Central America, the ocellated turkey, once decorated Maya temple walls and manuscripts. It was also eaten by the upper classes and by religious leaders.; An Apache legend describes the turkey as a bird of nourishment, but not in the form of meat. In the folktale, a turkey shakes his wings and produces four types of corn seeds, which are then planted, providing ample food for the community.

name: Vulture
description: As scavenger birds, vultures feed on carrion, the decaying flesh of animals. Because of this, we tend to associate them with death. In ancient Egypt, however, these birds were revered as symbols of rebirth. The goddess Nekhbet was depicted as a vulture, and ancient Egyptians believed all vultures were female, born from eggs without the need of male involvement. Thus, the birds were linked to motherhood, and they turned death into life by feeding on animal remains a circle of life, death, and rebirth. The wives of pharaohs, female pharaohs, and high ranking priestesses all wore vulture crowns to honor Nekhbet and invoke her protection.

name: Warbler
description: Two distinct families of warblers come from the Eastern and Western Hemispheres Sylvioidea are found in Eurasia and Africa, and Emberizoidea are found in the Americas, and while the two groups are not closely related, their songs are similar. Warblers are distinguished by their trilling calls, and therefore we call singers especially those who tend to embellish warblers.; The Japanese bush warbler, known in Japan as uguisu, is especially appreciated for its expressive song. Typically coinciding with the blooming of plum blossoms in February, the warblers mating call heralds the coming spring.

name: Waxwing
description: Named for the red markings on their wingtips said to resemble drops of sealing wax, these birds became associated with illness during the Middle Ages. Due to their migratory wanderings during cold winters, their sudden arrival in large flocks often coincided with outbreaks of the bubonic plague in parts of western Europe. While in reality waxwings arent especially likely to carry or spread disease, the association stuck. To this day, the Dutch call the waxwing pestvogel, meaning plague bird.

name: Weaverbird
description: Weaverbirds are named for their elaborate nests, woven from leaves, reeds, grasses, and twigs. The birds nest designs vary greatly among species. Some weaverbirds, aptly called sociable weavers, create apartment like nests with individual entrances for different mating pairs. Others build multiple nests in a single tree, and still others build solitary nests. The male weaverbird is the architect, and when his masterpiece is finished, he invites a potential mate to his palace. If the female approves, she mates with him; if she is not impressed, the male bird may try again, constructing another nest.

name: Woodpecker
description: Both male and female woodpeckers are known for drumming their beaks against hollow logs, dead trees, and even metal, creating a loud, reverberating noise that attracts a mate and declares their territory. Adapted to this behavior, the skull of the woodpecker is spongy, and its long tongue wraps around the brain to protect it. Likewise, the birds tough neck muscles and stiff beak absorb repetitive blows, preventing head injury.; In Norse mythology, the woodpecker is sacred to Thor, the god of thunder and lightning. Like Thor, the woodpecker wields his hammer, producing a sound that some liken to rolling thunder.

name: Wren
description: Little birds with loud voices, wrens are closely associated with L an Dreoil n, or Wren Day, on December 26. This Irish celebration traditionally involved hunting a wren, placing its body atop a decorated pole, and parading it through the village. Today, there is no hunt, and a stuffed wren is used in place of the live bird, but mummers, straw boys, or wren boys still dress in elaborate straw costumes to perform the ritual. Wren Day has been revived in parts of the United Kingdom, and similar traditions also have been observed in Spain and France. While the exact origins of this tradition are unknown, it is likely related to the winter solstice the robin, associated with warmth, defeats the wren, a bird of winter, restoring the sun for the new year.

name: A long the river during the qingming festival
description: On the way, we experience human stories eating, sleeping, romancing, arguing, socializing and above all shopping. The immense diversity of human connections is pulled together by the river that brings life into the city, and all classes, professions and characters are depicted with unbelievable precision.

name: The birth of venus
description: Sandro Botticellis poetic sense of beauty captivated the Florentine court, but it was his subject matter that distinguished him from other artists he was one of the first Western artists since classical times to depict nudes in non religious scenes.; The Birth of Venus 1485 was art for pleasure, not to serve God, and Botticellis depiction of an almost life sized nude was radical. 1 It wasnt Eve being expelled from the garden of Eden, shamed by her nudity. It wasnt the naked hordes sent to Hell in Dantes Inferno. In fact, it wasnt nudity as symbol of shame at all, or even sin, or wickedness; this was a celebration of the naked human form.

description: When they are closed, they form an image in green grey grisaille, showing the creation of the world as a flat disc enclosed in a transparent sphere, likely representing the Third Day of creation, when the separation of waters and land occurred, giving rise to the terrestrial Paradise or Eden. God appears in the top left hand corner, a tiny yet radiant figure in the darkness. His hands are raised, which is medieval code to tell us he is speaking, and he is reciting verse 9 of Psalm 33 For he spoke and it was done, for he commanded and it stood fast. The flat Earth and dome are peculiar to modern eyes, but can be explained by a translated passage in the Vulgate Bible which states that God created the sky under a dome. 4 Bosch would have been aware of this idea, as it was a standard artistic convention.
quotes: All of this points to the idea that this work was a conversation piece rather than a religious one

name: The garden of earthly delights (outer panels)
description: We know from infrared scans that Boschs original plan was a more classic image of God creating Eve from Adams rib. By shifting the focus of this panel to highlighting their union, he primed the audience for the central panels carnal depiction of Be fruitful and multiply. To Renaissance audiences, the link would have been obvious the Fall of Adam and Eve will inevitably lead to the crucifixion of Christ. This is underscored by the positioning of Adams feet, mirroring Christs while on the Cross.; Behind Christ is the Tree of Life, a dragon blood tree known for its dark red juice when cut. Its flat leaves represent Eucharistic wafers, while the grapes reference wine, establishing a direct association with the body and blood of Christ.; Though the Earthly Paradise appears peaceful at first glance, there is already the looming spectre of human sinfulness. The pool is populated with monstrous creatures who have already started to attack each other, foreshadowing the impending descent into chaos. One bird like monster consumes a toad, a classic symbol representing the Devils minions, associated with pestilence, which shows that the presence of evil exists even within the confines of Eden.; In the peculiar central fountain sits an owl another recurring motif for Bosch, found in eighteen of his works. This painting features six owls two in the left panel, three in the central panel and one in the right panel as the prince of Hell technically a nightjar. Contrary to its contemporary association with wisdom, in the Middle Ages the owl, a creature of the night hunting for prey, symbolized the Devil himself lying in wait for an opportunity to strike.; The left panel also features an unusual rock formation in the form of a weeping face. This is Golgotha, the site of the Crucifixion, according to the Gospels, where we see the serpent coiled around a palm tree. Four hundred years later Boschs painting would inspire the Surrealist movement, and Salvador Dal in particular.

name: The garden of earthly delights (adam and eve detail)
description: The central panel shows humanity indulging in earthly pleasures and desires, with imagery of excess and sensuality. Bosch shows us moral decay and the fleeting, hedonistic nature of a life detached from spiritual values.; If we go to the bottom right hand corner, we find a possible depiction of Adam. He is looking directly at us, as if he is the only one to understand whats going on, and pointing at Eve as if to say, This is how it started. Eve is holding the fruit she has just picked, and she is gagged by what looks like a communion wafer. Adam and Eve are also the only ones wearing clothes in the entire panel animal skins, which ties into the biblical story. 8; Everything in this paradise has some kind of sexual connotation; there is a voyeuristic edge to its supposed moral teachings.; The Earths fertility is represented by enormous and abundant soft fruits that are consumed with gusto, representing the fleeting nature of pleasure easy to rot decay. Hollowed out fruit was a symbol of female genitalia two cherries together, male genitalia. In the Middle Ages to pluck fruit was a euphemism for sex in Dutch, and blackberries, known for their multiple seeds, symbolized promiscuity. The empty mussel shells, peeled fruit, broken eggs and carcasses should be read, as with all the empty metaphors that Bosch employs, as emblematic of a lack of spirituality.; Every figure is engaged in their own activities; whether eating, chatting, dancing, groping or swimming, they are all individuals. There is heterosexual and homosexual activity, and even interspecies, in groups and in couples.; Bosch also shows a keen interest in the natural world, along with a powerful imagination when it came to improvising species he could only find in illuminated manuscripts and early printed matter. This was a time of great discoveries in the Indies and the New World of species of plants and animals.
quotes: The pool is populated with monstrous creatures who have already started to attack each other;This is a Hell that the medieval mind would have understood on many levels

name: The garden of earthly delights (prince of hell detail)
description: The climax of the painting is in the top right, a realistic portrayal of a city on fire that may well speak to Boschs childhood memories. A hostile army is seizing the city, and its gates are left wide open. Black silhouettes on horseback are galloping across a bridge while underneath, hundreds of wretches are drowning. This is a Hell that the medieval mind would have understood on many levels. 12 After all, death was all around them.

description: Within the soaring legends of Chinese mythology, the enigmatic creature known as Bai Ze emerges as a being of wisdom, purity, and otherworldly sight. Described in ancient texts as a white furred beast, Bai Zes appearance is striking a body resembling an ox, lion, or tiger, covered in thick fur as pale as mist, and often portrayed with multiple intelligent eyes, sometimes six or more, placed across its face and flanks. This multiplicity of vision symbolizes its ability to see hidden truths and recognize all supernatural beings, both benign and malignant.; The earliest known tale of Bai Ze appears in the historical and mythic chronicle known as the Shan Hai Jing The Classic of Mountains and Seas and was later repeated in Han Dynasty literature. According to legend, the creature was encountered by none other than the Yellow Emperor Huangdi, the semi divine ruler of ancient China who united the tribes of the Central Plain around 2600 BCE. During one of his sacred journeys to the eastern seacoast, the emperor came upon Bai Ze standing at the edge of a luminous mountain, cloaked in white mist, a radiant figure of peace and solemnity.; Recognizing its wisdom, the Yellow Emperor spoke with Bai Ze, who shared with him the knowledge of the 11, 520 types of supernatural creatures that existed across the world including spirits, demons, shapeshifters, and divine beings. Bai Ze did not merely name them but described their behaviors, habitats, strengths, and how they might be repelled or appeased. The emperor had this immense knowledge recorded into a now lost tome known as the Bai Ze Tu The Diagram of Bai Ze, which later became the basis for many exorcism manuals, talismanic practices, and medicinal demonology in Taoist and folk traditions.; Unlike fearsome monsters that challenge heroes, Bai Ze is a creature of guidance and clarity. Its role is not to battle, but to enlighten to act as a bridge between the world of mortals and the unseen realm of spirits. In Chinese thought, where harmony between all forces is central, Bai Ze represents the ideal of comprehension without fear, the principle that knowing ones enemy even if that enemy is invisible is the first step to maintaining balance. Its wisdom is not combative, but strategic, built upon deep spiritual awareness.; Throughout Chinese history, images of Bai Ze were used in protective amulets, especially during the Tang and Song Dynasties, to ward off evil spirits. It was said that simply possessing a drawing of Bai Ze, or even his name written on paper, was enough to prevent misfortune and illness brought on by demonic interference. In Taoist rituals, Bai Zes guidance was invoked by exorcists and spirit mediums seeking to identify troublesome forces causing affliction or imbalance within a household or individual.; Though Bai Ze is less widely known in the West, its legend continues in East Asian folklore, particularly in Japan, where it was reimagined in Edo period woodblock prints as Hakutaku, a similar creature of knowledge and exorcism. To this day, Bai Ze is honored as a protector of the learned, a patron of those who face darkness not with violence, but with vision. In its unblinking gaze, humanity finds not judgment, but clarity the gift of understanding a world far more mysterious than it seems.
quotes: White beast of divine Knowledge

name: Bixie - ??
description: From the carved gates of imperial tombs to the silent corridors of ancient palaces, the image of Bixie lingers like a watchful breath of stone. A creature of impossible grace, it bears the strength of a lion and the poise of a dragon, its wings unfurled in eternal vigilance. Where it stands, evil spirits scatter; where it flies, corruption cannot follow. To the ancients, Bixie was more than guardian it was the embodiment of virtues defense against decay.; The legend of Bixie traces its origin to the Han dynasty, when sculptors began adorning imperial tombs with hybrid beasts that bridged the human and celestial realms. The word bixie means to ward off evil, and the creatures name became its purpose. It was said that the gods themselves had molded the first of its kind from the breath of the Yellow Dragon, gifting it to mortals as a protector of the souls passage between worlds. Unlike fierce tigers or serpents, Bixie was guardian through purity power drawn from balance, not blood.; Ancient artisans carved its likeness from limestone and jade, placing them in pairs to flank sacred thresholds. Each statues gaze was fixed outward, wings poised to take flight, mouths slightly open as if whispering warnings to malevolent forces. Some were found buried beside emperors, their faces turned west toward the setting sun, a symbol of watchful peace over the journey beyond. The softness of their lines and the strength of their stance conveyed both serenity and strength, a union of gentleness and authority rarely seen in mythic beasts.; Bixies physical form harmonizes opposing elements. It bears the lions body and paws, a dragons scaled hide, and the wings of an immortal bird. Horns curve backward from its brow like river waves frozen in jade, and its eyes gleam with the clarity of dew. The creatures presence was said to calm tempests, silence demons, and bless the foundations of temples. Some traditions claimed that those who dreamed of Bixie would awaken freed from curses or grief, as if the creatures wings had brushed sorrow from their hearts.; In ritual use, Bixie often appeared alongside its kin, the Tianlu both members of a celestial pair that governed prosperity and protection. While Tianlu gathered wealth, Bixie dispersed evil, ensuring the households balance. Temples to the West and South of ancient capitals bore carvings of these companions as spirit guardians, charged with keeping unseen malice from entering the city gates. In later folk belief, the name Bixie itself became a charm; amulets and embroidered cloth bore the two characters to repel misfortune.; During the Tang and Song periods, scholars compared the creature to righteous officials who upheld integrity amid corruption. Bixie appeared in poetry as a symbol of incorruptible loyalty majestic, silent, and unyielding. In Ming tombs, its wings broadened, its expression softened, and its form evolved into a messenger between earth and sky. The people began to see in its image not only defense against evil, but the promise of transcendence.; To modern eyes, they appear timeless neither beast nor deity, but the breath of devotion turned to stone. In museums, their gaze meets ours as it once met the western horizon calm, eternal, and unafraid. Even now, when the wind moves gently through courtyards and temples, it is said that Bixies unseen wings still stir the dust, guarding the thresholds of the living and the dead alike.
quotes: Protector against misfortune

name: Fenghuang - ??
description: In the first light of creation, when the world was still song and smoke, the Fenghuang rose from the breath of heaven and earth entwined. It was neither wholly bird nor spirit, but the balance of all five elements made living a creature of air and flame, whose feathers shimmered with the colors of peace. Wherever it alighted, the ground became fertile, rivers cleared, and nations knew prosperity. To glimpse it was to know that the world stood in harmony.; The name Fenghuang once referred to two beings Feng, the male, and Huang, the female united as one eternal pair. Over time their duality merged into a single being, symbol of perfect balance between yin and yang. The oldest legends trace it to the Shang and Zhou dynasties, when bronze vessels bore its curling silhouette, long before the written word could fix its name. Its cry was said to contain five notes that summoned the winds of heaven, carrying blessings across the empire.; In form, the Fenghuang gathered the noblest parts of all creatures the cocks comb, the swallows face, the snakes neck, the fishs tail, and the peacocks brilliance. Its wings bore the pattern of virtue benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faith each rendered in hue and motion. When it flew, its plumage cast a thousand colors like sunlight on rippling silk; when it landed, even the fiercest beasts bowed in stillness. Unlike the phoenix of Western flame, this bird did not burn to be reborn it endured to preserve balance.; Legends tell that the Fenghuang appears only in times of peace and moral rule. During eras of corruption or war, it vanished beyond the firmament, unwilling to tread upon soiled lands. Emperors once claimed its visitation as divine approval of their virtue; empresses wore its likeness in gold and jade as the embodiment of feminine power and heavenly grace. On imperial thrones, the dragon and phoenix faced one another, eternal consorts ruling the worlds dual nature yangs command and yins harmony.; Its presence filled the rituals of the court. Ceremonial robes shimmered with embroidered phoenixes, wings spread in blessing. Musicians carved its image upon zithers to invoke refinement of spirit, and poets praised it as the voice of dawn that stirs kings to justice. In marriage rites, the Fenghuang symbolized union untainted by pride or greed a love that mirrored cosmic order. Where the dragon breathed thunder, the phoenix answered with song.; As dynasties passed, the birds meaning deepened. In Taoist and Confucian thought alike, it became the living embodiment of the Ways perfection strength tempered by compassion, power bound to virtue. Artisans painted its feathers in patterns that mimicked flowing clouds, weaving it into textiles and porcelain, each line a prayer for peace. In the Ming and Qing courts, it crowned empress headdresses, its golden wings trembling lightly as if stirred by unseen wind.; Even beyond the imperial walls, the people carried the Fenghuang in their hearts. Farmers painted it on doors to invite harmony into their homes; scholars inked it in scrolls as a metaphor for moral clarity. It came to represent all that endures without force, all that shines without consuming. To dream of its shadow was to awaken blessed, to feel the turning of ones fate toward gentler horizons.

name: Bai suzhen - ???
description: When spring rains fall over the broken stones of Hangzhous bridges, her story returns Bai Suzhen, the White Serpent, whose love defied heaven itself. She was once a spirit of the waters of Mount Emei, a serpent who cultivated for centuries beneath the moon until compassion transformed her into a woman of transcendent grace. In her, natures magic found its most human shape a being born of river and storm, seeking warmth not from sun or fire, but from the fragile heart of mortal love.; Her legend begins in the Tang dynasty, when a wandering scholar named Xu Xian met a mysterious lady on the banks of West Lake. She carried herself with such serenity that even the willows bowed. Bai Suzhen, drawn to him by the memory of kindness in a former life, took human form to be at his side. They wed beneath the peach blossoms, their bond defying the laws that separated spirits from men. For a time, heaven itself seemed to hold its breath, watching this union of mortal and divine.; Yet their happiness stirred the wrath of the monk Fahai, guardian of the Golden Mountain Temple, who saw in Bai Suzhens serpent nature a transgression against the cosmic order. He warned Xu Xian that his wife was a demon, but the scholar, blinded by both doubt and love, could not reconcile the woman he knew with the spirit she truly was. During the Dragon Boat Festival, Fahai tricked him into giving her realgar wine poison to serpents. Bai Suzhen collapsed, her form unraveling into a white snake so vast and radiant it blotted out the sky.; Shamed and heartbroken, she fled to the waters of West Lake, carrying within her a son yet unborn. Fahai, fearing her power, imprisoned her beneath Leifeng Pagoda, sealing her with sacred spells. There she remained for years, her sorrow echoing through the stones, her tears turning into lilies that bloomed each spring. Xu Xian, repentant, devoted himself to prayer until the heavens finally softened. The pagoda collapsed, and Bai Suzhen rose again from the waves, her spirit freed but forever marked by loves endurance.; In the moral weave of Chinese mythology, Bai Suzhen embodies the paradox of virtue within transgression. Though a spirit by birth, she represents the purity of human feeling a devotion so profound it bridged the boundary between heaven and earth. Her serpent form, feared for millennia as omen of danger, became in her story a vessel of compassion. Through her, the old image of the snake as deceiver was transfigured into one of wisdom, resilience, and grace.; Temples and operas retell her legend as both caution and consolation. In Hangzhou, worshippers still visit the Broken Bridge where she first met Xu Xian, offering incense for enduring love. Folk painters depict her with the Green Snake, Xiaoqing, her loyal companion and foil a spirit of fierce temper who balanced Bai Suzhens gentleness. Together, they became symbols of sisterhood, courage, and the right to choose love despite divine decree. Their story passed through song, shadow play, and porcelain, always renewed like the rain that bore her name.; To Taoist scholars, Bai Suzhens tale reflected the cosmic dance of yin and yang the serpents fluid strength representing the yielding power of the feminine, the human heart embodying the warmth that softens fate. To poets, she was a metaphor for enlightenment through emotion a truth reached not by withdrawal but by the willingness to feel deeply, even at the cost of pain. Her beauty was not of adornment but of transformation; her love, a bridge between illusion and awakening.
quotes: Spirit of devotion and love

name: Dongyue - shen - ????
description: At the heart of the eastern mountains where morning light first touches the world, Dongyue Shen reigns Lord of the Eastern Peak, master of Mount Tai, and judge of the mortal soul. He is both mountain and monarch, the still axis between heaven and hell, whose command governs the rhythm of birth, death, and renewal. In his shadow the dead pause, the living pray, and even gods defer to the weight of his decree. Mount Tai, sacred since the dawn of dynasties, has long been the ladder between worlds. Its slopes were said to be the first to rise from the sea when the earth was formed, its summit a throne where heaven stooped to greet the soil. From these heights, Dongyue Shen rules as arbiter of cosmic order, his jurisdiction spanning not only life and death but the very structure of destiny. Emperors climbed its paths to receive legitimacy from the heavens; peasants climbed to beg mercy for their ancestors souls. The earliest traces of his worship appear in the Zhou and Han dynasties, when the eastern mountain became synonymous with vitality and renewal. In those ages, Dongyue Shens form was elemental a spirit of the land who could shake rivers into obedience and awaken spring from stone. As the centuries passed, he evolved into a majestic ruler of the underworlds upper courts, presiding over the Ten Kings of Hell and commanding the celestial bureaucracy that recorded every breath and every deed of humankind. His temples rose wherever death met life in city gates, mountain passes, and river fords. Inside, colossal murals depicted him enthroned amid a retinue of scribes, demons, and heavenly attendants, each recording the souls passage through judgment. In one hand he held the scroll of names, in the other the brush of verdict. It was believed that those who lived with righteousness would be granted swift passage through his halls, their spirits escorted upward by cranes; while the deceitful would linger, weighed down by the ink of their sins. Rituals dedicated to Dongyue Shen were acts of profound reverence. On the first day of the second lunar month, offerings of incense, rice wine, and paper effigies were carried up mountain paths at dawn. Monks recited scriptures of salvation while families bowed three times toward the east, invoking his mercy to extend the lifespans of the living and ease the burdens of the dead. In imperial ceremonies, the emperor himself would face Mount Tai to announce victories, births, or omens, seeking the mountain lords witness to every turning of fate. Taoist scholars viewed Dongyue Shen as the manifestation of equilibrium the perfect union of yin and yang embodied in the steadfastness of earth. He was both merciful and unyielding, both nurturer and judge. His dominion reached beyond moral retribution to cosmic harmony; through him, the elements remained aligned and the boundaries between realms intact. To meditate upon his presence was to feel the still gravity of existence itself, the silence that underlies all movement. In later literature and drama, Dongyue Shen became the silent figure behind a thousand mortal stories the unseen adjudicator who restores justice when the world falters. His court mirrored the structure of an empire, complete with ministers of birth, death, punishment, and reward, reflecting the conviction that divine order and human order were one. Artists painted him with eyes that gazed beyond illusion, as though seeing not the flesh of men but the flame of their intentions.
quotes: Keeper of Souls;The Great Emperor of the Eastern Peak

name: Feng popo - ???
description: When the sky grows restless and the leaves tremble before a sudden gale, it is said that Feng Po Po, the Lady Wind, has stirred from her cloud borne dwelling. Neither goddess of wrath nor mere spirit of weather, she is the breath of the sky itself ancient, unpredictable, and endlessly compassionate in her wildness. Riding her great tiger through the air, she carries a sack woven of starlight, and within it, the winds of the world. When she opens it, tempests are born; when she closes it, silence returns. Her legend winds back to the earliest dynasties, when farmers watched the shifting heavens and named the unseen force that moved them. In the beginning, wind was a nameless mystery, but over time it found its matron Feng Po Po, the Lady who Commands the Air. Her name means Madam Wind or Grandmother Wind, a figure both nurturing and formidable. Some say she was once a celestial attendant to the Jade Emperor; others claim she is older still, a remnant of primordial creation the sigh the universe exhaled after it was made. In appearance, she is described as an elderly woman, her hair long and white as cirrus clouds, her face lined with wisdom rather than age. Though she seems frail, her strength is boundless. Her tiger mount embodies raw power and fearlessness, while her sack contains the delicate balance of the natural world. The smallest breath she releases becomes a spring breeze, carrying the scent of peach blossoms; a careless tug can summon a typhoon. Her laughter, rare and echoing, is said to travel across a thousand li, stirring bamboo and bending rivers in its wake. Through the centuries, Feng Po Pos presence was both revered and feared. Sailors prayed to her before setting out to sea, burning incense and releasing paper birds to guide her favor. Farmers offered rice and tea at hill shrines, asking for soft rains and gentle breezes. In contrast, those who forgot to show gratitude risked her displeasure an unseasonable storm, a harvest toppled by wind. She was not cruel, but balance was her law; every gust that nourished one land could scour another clean. Taoist texts and folk songs alike portray her as the embodiment of the Daos dual motion soft yet mighty, invisible yet ever present. The wind she commands is not merely air, but the vital qi that flows through all living things. In this sense, Feng Po Po is the living symbol of transformation, of movement that sustains existence. Her tiger, guardian of courage and direction, represents control over chaos. Together they form the perfect union of stillness within motion the world breathing in and out. In art and literature, she often appears in moments of change a scroll painting where petals scatter before her passing, or a poems final line describing her sigh dissolving into rain. Unlike deities of flame or thunder, she does not seek worship but remembrance. Her work is unseen yet felt, her story carried by the very air that sustains all life. The ancients said that when she rides unseen through the night, mortals hear only the rustle of leaves and think it is the world turning in its sleep. Over time, the Lady Wind has become a quiet guardian of fate. Her image adorns amulets for travelers and kites that rise with springs first warmth. She is invoked by those who seek freedom, her breath guiding sails, journeys, and dreams alike. Though her power can summon ruin, her purpose is always restoration she clears the dust so light can return.
quotes: Mistress of storms

name: Jingwei - ??
description: Each dawn over the eastern seas, a small bird cries a plaintive song sharp, relentless, and filled with longing. The wind carries her voice across the waves, a vow repeated since the dawn of time. This is Jingwei, the daughter of Emperor Yan, who once drowned in the seas cold embrace and rose again transformed, her sorrow made flesh and feathers. Though her body is frail, her will defies eternity. Day after day, she carries pebbles and twigs to the ocean, striving to fill it and reclaim what was taken from her.; In the earliest chronicles, her tale is told as both tragedy and testament. Once she was N wa, a young princess of radiant beauty and curiosity. Drawn by the horizons shimmer, she ventured beyond her fathers domain and was claimed by the sea in a storm that no mortal could endure. The ocean, vast and indifferent, swallowed her cries. Yet death did not end her. From the depths rose a bird of fiery spirit, its feathers tinged with the colors of sunrise, its song a promise of resistance. She named herself Jingwei, meaning Spirit of Resolution, and swore to conquer the waves that had consumed her.; The ancients saw in her transformation not vengeance but purpose. Jingweis endless labor carrying twigs and stones in her beak, dropping them into the boundless sea was the very image of perseverance against the impossible. The sea mocked her futility, yet she did not waver. For thousands of years, poets and philosophers have repeated her name to honor the defiance that outlasts despair. Her struggle became a mirror for humanity itself fragile before the universe, yet capable of infinite persistence.; Descriptions of Jingwei vary through dynasties. In some texts she is as small as a sparrow, with plumage of red tipped wings and white throat, the colors of sunrise and foam. In others she glows with a faint halo of flame, a divine spark refusing to fade. Her eyes, dark and luminous, reflect both grief and serenity. No mortal wind can deter her, and no god forbids her quest. The twigs and stones she gathers from distant mountains and forests are offerings to memory, each drop into the water an act of devotion to what was lost.; Her story resonated deeply with scholars and dreamers alike. To the Confucians, she embodied filial piety taken beyond life, her vow born from love for her father and homeland. To Taoists, she was a parable of harmony through endurance the understanding that even futility holds meaning when it aligns with ones inner truth. And to poets, she was the symbol of courage in loneliness, the unyielding pulse of life within endless sorrow. In her small wings lived the echo of a heart that refused to yield to fate.; In art, Jingweis image became a motif of transformation. Han dynasty bronzes depict her hovering above curling waves, a pebble suspended beneath her beak. In painted scrolls she flies against the sun, her form radiant with quiet determination. The story was retold through song and opera, her cry Jingwei, Jingwei a call of hope disguised as mourning. Even emperors found solace in her legend, seeing in her the perseverance required to govern a world as shifting as the sea.
quotes: Daughter of loss

name: Kungpeng - ???
description: At the edge of the northern sea, where the waters blur into cloud and the horizon folds upon itself, something stirs in the depths an ancient fish so vast that even the mountains tremble in its wake. The sages called it Kun, a creature of impossible scale whose shadow darkens leagues of water at once. When the seasons turn and the deep stirs with light, the Kun sheds its form, rising through the storm as the Peng, a bird whose wings stretch across the vault of heaven. The flight of Kunpeng is the first metaphor of freedom; its transformation, the universe learning to dream.; In the Zhuangzi, where the story first unfolds, the philosopher writes of a wind that lifts from the north and bears this creature thousands of miles into the azure sky. No cage could ever contain it, no measure could define its scale. The Peng rises ninety thousand li high, soaring above clouds, piercing through the strata of heaven until the sun itself becomes a spark beneath its wings. Its flight is not a journey but a revelation the boundless Dao made visible in the form of living motion.; When the Kun slumbers beneath the frozen seas, the world feels smaller, its energy condensed and still. But when it awakens and transforms, creation ripples outward, waves breaking against the pillars of heaven. Fishermen on distant shores glimpse whirlpools turning to sky, the deep lifting itself into air, and they whisper prayers for mercy. Yet Kunpeng is no harbinger of disaster; it is the shifting face of infinity, the proof that every being contains its opposite, and that transformation is the universes truest act of faith.; No one has ever seen the whole of its body only fragments reflected in sea and cloud. Its wings are said to be made of the same breath that moves storms, its feathers etched with constellations. When it moves, tides and seasons follow; when it rests, even the stars seem to hold still. The Daoists saw in Kunpeng the essence of the Way itself form without form, change without end. For them, its metamorphosis from fish to bird was not miracle but truth to transcend limitation, one must accept the art of becoming.; In later ages, poets wrote of its transformation as the allegory of the human spirit. Li Bai compared his own ambitions to its flight, yearning to rise beyond the smallness of courtly life. Scholars saw in Kunpeng the souls capacity for enlightenment, its breaking free from the confines of the self. Artists painted it as both dream and paradox the creature whose wings define the horizon, whose depth defies measure, whose journey begins and ends in the same breath.; Temples near northern rivers carved its likeness upon their stones, not as an idol but as reminder. The priests said its dual forms embodied yin and yang the depths of water and the expanse of sky, patience and motion, introspection and revelation. To meditate upon Kunpeng was to listen to the sound of the worlds heartbeat slow, vast, and eternal. Some even believed that each soul, through countless lifetimes, must learn the secret of its flight, to rise from the sea of illusion into the sky of clarity.; And so the legend endures a creature neither wholly bird nor fish, but everything in between the sea that dreams of sky and the sky that remembers water. When thunder rolls over distant waves, it is said that Kunpeng is stirring, stretching its wings before another ascension. The ancient texts say it flies where the wind is born, its feathers brushing eternity.
quotes: Embodiment of transformation

name: Lei gong chongsheng
description: When the heavens darken and the air trembles with a pulse that feels older than the world, Lei Gong Chongsheng rises. His wings split the clouds, his hammer resounds across valleys, and every heart pauses half in fear, half in awe. He is the Duke of Thunder, the living embodiment of celestial justice, the one whose sound shapes the will of heaven. To hear his voice is to hear the verdict of the divine itself.; Legends say he was born not from flesh but from sound. When the universe first uttered thunder, its echo took form in the shape of a man with the face of a hawk and the body of a warrior, clothed in scales of stormlight. From his breath came the first winds, from his heart the pulse of rain. In the days when the world was still unformed, he struck his drum to awaken the sleeping sky, and the rhythm of existence began. Even the gods listened because in Lei Gongs thunder lay the truth of consequence.; His duty is sacred and merciless to strike those who transgress the cosmic order. It is said that when a mortal commits a hidden crime murder unrepented, deceit unspoken Lei Gong hears it as a discord in the harmony of heaven. He flies upon thunderclouds, drum strapped to his back, mallet raised high. Each blow sends a bolt racing down to the guilty, splitting arrogance and shadow alike. Yet he strikes not from cruelty, but from necessity. To him, thunder is not destruction it is purification.; In every depiction, his form brims with tension muscles taut as drawn bowstrings, wings coiled with electric feathers, eyes glowing with the light that precedes rain. His hands bear a stone mallet and chisel, tools with which he carves divine judgment into the air. When he beats the drum of heaven, lightning follows his rhythm, rain obeys his tempo. The Taoists called him Chongsheng, Holy Voice, for his roar was the note that binds heaven and earth to moral order. Without his thunder, the world would lose its pulse.; His consort, Dianmu the Mother of Lightning rides beside him in a flash of gold. Together they create the storms symphony she illuminates the sins of men, and he strikes where her light reveals. Their union is both tender and terrifying an eternal dance of cause and consequence, of vision and judgment. When their storm descends, the world is scoured clean, yet when it ends, the earth glistens anew, reborn beneath their mercy.; Farmers once prayed to him before the planting season, asking that his thunder break the soil but spare their homes. In every rumble of the rainy months, they heard his measured wrath and his warning that balance, once broken, must always be restored. Monks chanted his name in temples perched high upon cliffs, believing the sound of their bells echoed his own eternal drum. The rhythm of thunder became a metaphor for conscience a reminder that unseen wrongs will one day call down their echo from the sky.; Through centuries of worship, Lei Gongs image evolved. In the Ming and Qing dynasties, he became the stern general of Heavens law, presiding over celestial courts that judged spirits and mortals alike. His likeness adorned shrines dedicated to justice; magistrates swore oaths before his image to remain impartial and true. To betray such vows invited the very storm to ones threshold. Yet beneath his fierceness lay compassion, for Lei Gong punished only to restore harmony his voice, though terrible, was born of care.

name: Lianhu gui
description: On still summer nights, when lotus ponds lie heavy with the scent of rain, a pale figure is said to walk across the water. Her feet make no ripple, her voice is softer than wind, and each step leaves a bloom in her wake. This is the Lianhu Gui the Lotus Ghost a spirit born from heartbreak and devotion, forever bound to the purity she could not attain in life. Though her tale begins in tragedy, it unfolds like the flower that bears her name sorrow opening into grace.; Long ago, when dynasties still cast their reflection on the rivers skin, there lived a maiden who tended the lotus ponds of a temple near Suzhou. Her name is lost to time, but she was said to have been gentle, devoted, and untouched by worldly desires. Each dawn, she waded through the lilies to gather blossoms for the altar of Guanyin, her prayers rising with the morning mist. But her heart, though pure, was not empty. A passing scholar, whose kindness matched her own, stole her heart with a poem written on a petal. Their love, though silent, bound heaven and earth in secret bloom.; When the scholar left and did not return, the temple whispered that fate had tested her. Each day she waited by the waters edge, her reflection fading thinner with the years. One evening, as storms gathered over the mountains, she walked into the pond with arms full of lotuses and never came back. When the monks searched for her, they found only blossoms floating where she had stood and the faint scent of incense rising through the rain.; That night, the ponds came alive with strange light. A womans shadow glided across the surface, her robes made of petals, her hair glistening with dew. The water rippled though no wind blew, and from beneath the lilies came a voice, gentle and mournful, reciting the same verse she once loved. The villagers called her Lianhu Gui, the Lotus Ghost, a spirit neither cursed nor vengeful but devoted bound to the world not by anger, but by memory.; Her form, described in countless tales, is as fragile as moonlight a figure of translucent beauty, her face veiled in sorrow, her garments unfolding like blossoms in water. The air around her smells of rain and temple smoke. Wherever she appears, the lilies bloom out of season, their white petals drifting toward her as though in recognition. She does not speak to frighten, only to remind. Those who have heard her song say it brings tears before sleep and peace upon waking.; To Taoist mystics, the Lotus Ghost became a symbol of purification through emotion the idea that suffering, when borne with love, transforms into transcendence. The lotus that grows from mud yet remains unstained mirrors her essence human pain reborn as spiritual clarity. In temple murals and opera, she is often depicted alongside Guanyin, offering a lotus to the bodhisattva as a prayer for souls still caught in longing. Some say her devotion was rewarded, that every time a lotus opens, a fragment of her spirit breathes anew into the world.; Travelers tell that on quiet nights by old temple ponds, one might see her reflection before the moon appears pale, luminous, and smiling faintly, as though remembering something kind. The brave leave offerings of flowers or ink written verses, and by morning, the wind scatters the petals, taking the wish with it. Her presence lingers not as dread but as serenity a guardian of unspoken love, of dreams too gentle to die.
quotes: Spirit of Purity

name: Long wang - ???
description: When thunder rolls across a tranquil sea and waves rise without wind, the Dragon King has stirred in his palace beneath the depths. He is Long Wang, ruler of all waters and guardian of the rain, a god whose patience can nurture nations or drown them in his wrath. To sailors he is salvation, to farmers he is lifeblood, to the impious he is judgment an immortal who holds dominion over the veins of the earth.; Ancient scriptures speak of four Dragon Kings, each governing one of the cardinal seas Ao Guang of the East, Ao Qin of the South, Ao Run of the West, and Ao Shun of the North. Together they form the aqueous empire of heaven, their palaces carved from coral and luminous pearl. Above them reigns the Jade Emperor, yet even he relies on their power, for rain itself answers their command. When drought or flood threatened the mortal realm, emperors knelt to Long Wang, offering silk and jade to appease his tides.; Legends say the Dragon Kings body mirrors the nature of his realm vast and fluid, ever changing. His scales flash the colors of sunrise over water turquoise, emerald, and pale gold while his eyes shift from tranquil blue to storm lit crimson. He rides currents as easily as others breathe air, and his voice echoes through rainstorms as low thunder. In the calm of the deep he is a scholar; in tempest, a general; in silence, a judge whose wisdom has no shore.; Countless stories tell of his dealings with mortals. Once, a fisherman returned a captured turtle to the sea and was invited to Long Wangs palace, where pillars of mother of pearl gleamed brighter than moonlight. The Dragon King rewarded him with a gem that could summon gentle rain. Another tale tells of an emperor who broke his vow of reverence; when his armies marched against sacred waters, the tides rose overnight and erased them from history. Such stories remind that the Dragon Kings mercy and fury flow from the same source the necessity of balance.; In Taoist cosmology, Long Wang governs the vital element of water, the essence of adaptability. His domain symbolizes the hidden power of softness the way rivers carve stone, the way rain nourishes root and mountain alike. Through him, the doctrine of yielding strength becomes manifest; the dragons dance beneath the waves mirrors the Taos unseen current guiding all existence. To honor him was to respect the equilibrium between heavens order and the wildness of nature.; Temples dedicated to the Dragon Kings dotted the coasts and riverbanks of every dynasty. Worshippers carried offerings of incense, shells, and miniature ships, praying for safe passage and bountiful harvests. During festivals, priests raised banners painted with azure dragons, and dancers imitated their winding grace, summoning rain with drums that mimicked the thunder of his realm. In drought, children carried paper dragons through the streets, singing for his compassion; in flood, the same songs begged his restraint.; Across literature and opera, Long Wang appears as both benefactor and sovereign of terrifying dignity. In the Journey to the West, he aids the monk Xuanzang on his pilgrimage, granting protection through his dragon prince son. Yet even heroes tread carefully in his presence, for his justice is ancient and impartial. To speak falsehood before him is to drown in ones own words; to act with purity is to find calm waters under ones boat.
quotes: Master of the four seas

name: Ying long - ??
description: When clouds gather in ranks like an army and the wind hums the ancient tune of power, Yinglongs wings unfold across the sky. His vast shadow rolls over mountains and rivers, and thunder answers his heartbeat. He is the Winged Dragon elder of storms, herald of justice, and the only dragon said to bear wings among his kind. Through his flight, heaven remembers its promise to nourish the earth; through his vengeance, it restores the balance of divine law.; In the age when gods and mortals still shared the same horizon, the Yellow Emperor waged war against the rebel Chiyou, whose breath raised mists of blood and smoke. The battle raged without end until Yinglong descended from the heavens, wings outspread, eyes blazing with lightning. With a single roar, he summoned torrents that drowned the rebel armies and cleansed the battlefield of corruption. The Emperors victory was won not through might alone, but through Yinglongs mercy his storm washing away the poison that defied the natural order. From that day, he was known as the ally of emperors, the dragon who fought for justice, not dominion.; Yet even the most divine must bear burden for their deeds. The old texts tell that after he unleashed his great floods, Yinglongs wings grew heavy with the weight of heavens grief. He descended to dwell among rivers and clouds, stripped of some of his celestial power, yet never stripped of purpose. Where others slept beneath the sea, he continued his work summoning rain to nourish crops, guiding floods away from villages, marking the passage of seasons with the steady rhythm of his wings.; In form, Yinglong is neither beast nor god but the meeting point of both. His wings shimmer like scales of light, feathered yet edged in armor. His body winds across the horizon like a river of azure silk, and his claws gleam with the color of polished jade. Lightning follows him not as weapon but as herald. In some depictions he bears the sun on one shoulder and the moon on the other, symbols of perfect balance between light and shadow. When he roars, the air itself bends; when he sleeps, clouds gather above him as guardians.; Worshippers in the early dynasties built shrines along riverbanks and high cliffs, where rain often first touched the earth. Farmers burned incense beneath banners painted with wings of blue and gold, pleading for temperate weather and protection from flood. Scholars, too, saw in him the symbol of enlightened strength action guided by wisdom, power restrained by compassion. In Taoist alchemy, his flight represented transcendence the spirit rising above its earthly vessel to rejoin the eternal current of the Dao.; But Yinglong was also a god of vengeance. When mortals desecrated sacred lands or defied divine harmony, he would darken the skies in warning. His storms, though terrifying, never struck without reason. To the faithful, the rolling thunder was not punishment but remembrance a voice reminding humankind that reverence for balance is the price of peace. His rain could erase, but also restore; his lightning could destroy, yet it could also illuminate. He was not merely the hand of heaven, but its conscience.; The Han carved his likeness into tomb walls as guardian of the departed; the Tang poets wrote of his wings reflecting dawn and dusk alike, his flight a metaphor for the immortal soul ascending beyond fate. He was the dream of transcendence, the symbol of the unbroken link between the celestial and the mortal, between storm and renewal.
quotes: Avenger of Heaven

name: Zhulin shen
description: When wind moves through the bamboo groves, it sings a voice that is not of man or beast but of something eternal soft, rhythmic, and knowing. Those who pause to listen may hear within it the whisper of Zhulin Shen, the Spirit of the Bamboo Forest, whose breath fills the stillness between rustling leaves. She is not a goddess to be worshipped in temples, but a guardian to be found in quiet places, a soul that speaks of endurance through grace and strength through gentleness.; The ancients believed that where bamboo grew, purity and order followed. Unlike other trees, it bends but does not break, hollow yet unempty, upright yet yielding virtues that mirror the heart of the Dao. In the oldest villages, when the groves swayed together like waves, elders said that Zhulin Shen was passing through, brushing her fingers across each stalk to remind them to stand tall even in the storm. The sound of her movement, a low sigh of wind and whisper, was her only prayer.; Some say she was once a mortal woman, a poet who withdrew into the bamboo forest to escape the vanity of kings and courts. She wrote verses so serene that the wind itself envied her. When she died, the grove refused to wither, and the spirit of bamboo absorbed her calm. Others believe she is far older a primordial essence born from the first breath of spring, the memory of when the world still spoke in green. Whatever her origin, she is now the soul of quiet persistence, watching over all who seek clarity amid chaos.; In the Book of Mountains and Seas, it is written that the spirits of plants learn from her the pine its steadfastness, the plum its courage to bloom in cold, and bamboo its ability to endure with dignity. Where she dwells, corruption fades, and the air carries the scent of rain even in drought. Travelers who lose their way among bamboo groves often find the path opening suddenly before them, the sound of footsteps fading into tranquil silence. Such moments are said to be her kindness guidance without display, compassion without voice.; In art, Zhulin Shen appears as a woman woven from mist and leaves. Her robes ripple with light like sunlight through green water. Artists paint her holding a bamboo flute, for it is said that her music teaches patience to the restless and humility to the proud. Scholars often kept such paintings above their desks, believing her calm presence would protect their thoughts from corruption and keep their hearts aligned with truth. To dream of her was to awaken wiser than before.; During storms, when bamboo bends nearly to breaking, the people whisper her name. She does not shield the grove from wind; she teaches it to move with it. For this reason, she became an emblem of moral and spiritual integrity the strength that bows without falling. The Confucians revered her as the living symbol of virtue, the Daoists as embodiment of natural balance, and the poets as muse of purity that endures without armor.
