In eulogiz ing Burrows, LIFE editor Ralph Graves wrote, I do not think it is demeaning to any other photographer in the world to say that Larry Burrows was the bravest, most dedicated war photographer I know of His dream was to stay until he could photograph a Vietnam at peace.

name: Saigon execution
description: The streets of Saigon were in chaos on February 1, 1968, two days into the Tet Offensive. An out of uniform soldier of the Viet Cong, Nguy n V n Lm, was captured and accused of the murder of a South Vietnamese colonel and his family. AP photographer Eddie Adams watched as Lm was marched into the street, where Brigadier General Nguyen Ngoc Loan lifted his. 38 revolver to Lms head and fired. Adamss photograph caught the precise moment when the bullet entered Lms skull. In the United States, the shocking brutality of the picture helped galvanize the antiwar move ment. Not only did it graphically demonstrate the savagery of war, but it added credence to the charges that military officials had lied when they said the U. S. had the conflict well under control. While all important photos have an afterlife, some are stranger than others. Adams won the Pulitzer Prize for this picture but grew uneasy with his role in taking it. Two lives were destroyed, he would say later, and I was getting paid for it. General Loan would say of his actions, If you hesitate, if you didnt do your duty, the men wouldnt follow you, but his life would be shadowed by the photograph. Loan eventually relocated to the United States and for a time owned and managed a pizza restaurant in Virginia. He closed it after tiring of being harassed by those who knew his story.

name: Criminal evidence
description: The horrors of torture at Abu Ghraib prison during the Iraq War were exposed in photos taken by the perpetrators of the crimes U. S. military personnel who gleefully snapped pictures of their ugly work. The photographs, first leaked and revealed in 2004, showed various atrocities, but it was this shot that became the symbol of the scandal and its most recognized image. The photo shows a hooded Iraqi prisoner later identified as Abdou Hussain Saad Faleh standing on a box, his fingers attached to dummy electrical wires. Faleh had been told by his tormentors that if he fell off the box, he would be electrocuted. The photographer responsible for this shot was Staff Sergeant Ivan L. Chip Frederick II, the highest ranking of the U. S. servicepeople charged in the beatings. After the ensuing trials, eleven soldiers were sentenced to prison; Frederick was given an eight and a half year sentence but was paroled after serving four years. The photo would gain additional notoriety when a different Abu Ghraib prisoner, Ali Shalal Quaissi, claimed in a 2006 front page New York Times article that he was the hooded man in the picture, earning him short lived attention until his story was proven false

name: Extraordinary situation
description: President Barack Obama and members of his national security team had huddled in a White House conference room on May 1, 2011, to watch video being sent by a drone hovering above a residence in Abbottabad, Pakistan. The mission to assassinate Osama Bin Laden, mastermind of the 9 11 terror attack, was in progress. White House photographer Pete Souza, crammed into a corner of the room, took this now iconic photo at 4 05 p. m. in Washington; it was dark of night in Pakistan. The photograph is titled Situation Room, but it was taken in a smaller room adjacent to the much larger and more formal conference room typically used. The crowded unease of the setting contributes to the palpable tension in the picture, as does the randomness of the seating, with the president tucked in back wearing his golf clothes Obama had played golf earlier that day to help deflect suspicions of anything unusual in the works. As Secretary of State Hillary Clinton would later say, Those were 38 of the most intense minutes.

name: Out of afghanistan
description: The image is instantly arresting an enormous plane holding a vast mass of Afghan men, women, and children. Despite the implausible sense of order and calm in the photo, it has emerged as a paradoxical symbol of the chaotic failures of the U. S. withdrawal from Afghanistan. The hurried pullout of American troops and sudden takeover by the Taliban had left Kabuls Hamid Karzai International Airport as the countrys lone island of escape for Americans and Afghans alike. The scene had been deadly and desperate. On August 15, 2021, a U. S. Air Force C 17 Globemaster III cargo plane was readied to load passengers approved for evacuation. But when the rear cargo doors of the plane opened, a huge crowd of frightened Afghans near the tarmac rushed the aircraft and pushed aboard. By the time the doors closed, 823 people were crammed inside. Due to the deterioriating situation at the airport, the crew quickly decided that rather than try to remove unauthorized refugees from the plane, it would be wiser simply to take off and proceed to the destination, Qatar. The photo, snapped by an Air Force photographer, created a sensation and is likely to endure as one of the most striking and unexpected images of the War in Afghanistan

name: Beckoning west
description: When Central Pacific Railroad president Leland Stanford swung a spike maul, knocked down a 17. 6 karat golden spike, and joined the two parts of the transcontinental railroad, on site telegraph operators at Promontory Summit, Utah, relayed the news and set off the first mass media event. San Franciscans greeted the report of the linking of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts with a 220 canon salute; New Yorks Trinity Church played the hymn Old Hundred; in Washington, D. C., President Ulysses S. Grant was handed a telegram that read, The last rail is laid Then, as Central Pacific chief engineer Samuel Montague and Union Pacifics Grenville Dodge shook hands, Andrew Joseph Russell who documented the lines construc tion captured the moment. Russells photograph of the nosing locomotives and proud work crews created an image that would entice Americans with the possibility of easier transcontinental travel. 53

name: First x-ray
description: Wilhelm Conrad R ntgen wanted to know the effects of cathode rays, streams of electromagnetic energy that emit negative electrodes. While experimenting in his lab, the University of W rzburg professor realized that the rays had passed through the glass tubes and caused a nearby sheet of paper to glow. R ntgen dubbed his discovery X rays, since their cause was unknown, and started taking X rays of inanimate objects to see what existed below the surface. Just before Christmas 1895, he positioned his wife Annas left hand and photographed her bones and wedding rings. R ntgens breakthrough not only won him the Nobel Prize in Physics it offered doctors an invaluable diagnostic tool. Anna R ntgen, though, took a more somber view of her husbands work, noting, I have seen my death.

name: Into the deep
description: While underwater photography started in the 1850s, pictures could only be taken in shallow areas. French zoologist Louis Marie Auguste Boutan sought to plumb further depths. To produce an image meant he had to devise a sealed box to encase a camera, photographic plates, a shutter, and a diaphragm, all adjusted by outside levers. He also needed a light source that didnt require oxygen, so he used a rubber ball that blew magnesium powder that could spark an electric charge. In 1899, Boutan lowered his 1, 000 pound camera into the waters off Frances Mediterranean coast, and at a depth of 165 feet recorded his colleague Emil Racovitza holding a sign that read PHOTOGRAPHIE SOUS MARINE French for under water photography. In a flash, Boutan offered the first hints of the wonders hidden in the deep blue sea

name: First flight
description: Dayton, Ohio, bicycle builders and shop owners Wilbur and Orville Wright loved to tinker, and for three years they spent months at a time near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, to take advantage of the brisk winds and soft landing shoreline to see if they could create a self propelled aircraft. They built the Flyer, and locals helped them test the wood, wire, and cloth Tinkertoy like contraption. On the morning of December 17, 1903, Wilbur set John Daniels next to a camera and told him to squeeze the pneumatic bulb that would trip the shutter if anything interesting happened. Orville then climbed into the Flyer. It slid down a track, took off, and covered 120 feet in 12 seconds. Daniels was so excited by the sight that he wasnt sure if he had photographed the event. It wasnt until the Wrights returned to Ohio a few weeks later and developed the glass plate that they realized they did, in fact, have proof that they had launched the age of flight

name: The aerial view
description: My pilot flew me over it, under and around it, to get the effect of the big plane looming large in the fore ground with the skyscrapers below, LIFE staff photographer Margaret Bourke White recalled of her venture shooting pictures of the sleek Douglas DC 4 as it soared above Manhattan, at a time when passenger flight was a new and wondrous phenomenon. In the course of documenting the worlds largest land transport plane, she also captured stunning views that before the age of aircraft had belonged only to the birds

name: The dna double helix
description: Since the 1860s, scientists had known that DNA contained the basic blueprint of life, but they had no idea what it looked like. Rosalind Franklin, a researcher at Londons King College, hoped to capture an image of the molecule. Using X ray diffraction and a 100 hour exposure, she produced this first ever image of a strand of DNA on her 51st try. Maurice Wilkins, a colleague with whom Franklin had a strained work relationship, showed rival researcher James Watson the photo. Upon seeing the distinctive X pattern, Watson later wrote, My mouth fell open, and my pulse began to race. He and his colleague James Crick understood that the shape is the signature for a helical form. From it they built a model of DNAs double helix strands winding around each other. When they completed their creation, Crick proclaimed in a pub that he had found the secret of life. For this, the men, including Wilkins, shared a Nobel Prize; Franklins critical role wasnt acknowleged until years after her death

name: Atop mount everest
description: More than a dozen climbers had already died trying to reach Mount Everests 29, 035 foot summit. Even so, Edmund Hillary, a New Zealander, and Tenzing Norgay of Nepal sought to brave the 100 mile an hour winds and yawning crevices to scale the worlds tallest peak. It proved to be a perilous climb. At one point, Hillary slid down 20 to 30 feet before realizing I could look down 10, 000 feet between my legs. When they arrived at the top, he recalled, We shook hands and then thumped each other on the back until forced to stop from lack of breath. The pair snapped photo graphic proof and ate some mint cake; Norgay made an offering to the gods of Everest, and they then headed down. It was an achievement of perseverance similar to Charles Lindberghs 1927 flight across the Atlantic. It also inspired many other climbers now, some 800 set off each year for the summit.

name: Earthrise
description: On Christmas Eve 1968, Apollo 8 rounded the moon. As lunar module pilot William Anders looked out the porthole, he exclaimed, Oh, my God Look at that picture over there Heres the Earth coming up. Wow, is that pretty He grabbed a Hasselblad camera, and while he floated, he snapped the first image of an earthrise. Wed come 240, 000 miles to see the moon, and it is the Earth that was really worth looking at, he recalled. While the Vietnam War raged below, a spaceman shared the peaceful beauty of the green blue speck of rock he believed should be thought of as a fragile Christmas tree ball. It was a place, he noted, that must be cared for. His photograph would go on to spark the environmental movement.

name: Moon walk
description: When Buzz Aldrin stepped out onto the moons Sea of Tranquility, he marveled at the satellites magnificent desolation. Fellow astronaut Neil Armstrong photographed him, and Armstrongs image, along with that of the lunar module, can be seen reflected in Aldrins visor. The picture, Aldrin said, was the result of an entirely serendipitous moment. But while the visit to another heavenly body resulted from technological advances and brought about what Armstrong called a giant leap for mankind, Apollo 11 s trip was ultimately made possible by curiosity. These and other images suddenly made more real the mysterious and alluring white sphere that humans had watched arc through the night sky for millennia.

name: The red planet
description: It took eleven months for Viking 1 to travel from Earth to Mars and become the first spacecraft to successfully land there. Within moments of setting down, it snapped images that took only four minutes to travel the more than 200 million miles back to Earth. While the folks at NASAs Mission Control knew they werent likely to see little green men, they were still mesmerized by their first peek at the rock strewn Red Planet. Some 16, 000 more photos by Viking 1 along with Viking 2, which would arrive soon after streamed across space over the next six years as the probes relayed information about the planets structure and composition. Viking 1 blazed the way for other missions, some arriving with roaming rovers, and set the stage for NASAs goal of sending humans to Mars by the 2030s.

name: A hole in the ozone
description: Without the high concentration of ozone molecules that make up the ozone layer which, at roughly nine to 22 miles above Earth, shields the planet from solar ultraviolet radiation life wouldnt exist. Scientists had long suspected that decom posing chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, emitted by such products as aerosol sprays, break down ozone molecules and thin the barrier. In 1985, the British Antarctic Survey discovered a hole above the Antarctic, offering proof. The unexpected finding forced developed nations to ban the manufacture of CFCs. In 2018, scientists observed that the decline in the use of the chemicals had lessened the destruction, and the ozone layer was expected to heal by mid century. But climate change appears to be slowing down the recovery. The hole grew larger in 2020 and 2021.

name: Pillars of creation
description: What looks like rising tendrils of otherworldly stalagmites are actually 30 trillion mile tall clouds of interstellar dust and hydrogen gas carved by high energy winds shooting from nearby stars. Floating in the Eagle Nebula 6, 500 light years away from Earth, they have for good reason been named the Pillars of Creation. These evaporating gaseous globules EGGs are hatcheries for the creation of new stars, and we can see them because of the Hubble Space Telescope. Orbiting far above the distortions caused by Earths atmosphere allowed Hubbles piano size Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 to not only record the birth of stars, but to capture images of colliding galaxies and the vastness of space.

name: Climate change
description: One of the clearest signs of global warming is the melting of the polar north. The ice loss not only endan gers Indigenous Arctic habitats and ways of life but speeds up coastal erosion and threatens the existence of polar bears, like this one strug gling across the ice north of Spitsbergen, Norway. Some 20, 000 to 30, 000 polar bears live in the wild. They primarily feed on seals, but the decline in ice makes it harder for the bears to hunt. A 2020 study revealed that at the current rate of tempera ture increase, the species will vanish by 2110. Polar bears have become the poster child of climate change, said P ter K. Moln r, an assistant professor in the University of Torontos department of biological sciences. Polar bears are already sitting at the top of the world; if the ice goes, they have no place to go. In this image, the bear seems forlorn as it navigates the changing landscape, a reaction many find all too relatable.

name: Meet the beatles
description: Photographer Harry Benson was trailing the Beatles for the Daily Express, and he was in their hotel suite when John Lennon remarked, That was some pillow fight we had the other night. Benson suggested they go at it again, and John demurred which turned out to be a ruse so he could sneak up on Paul McCartney and get in the first blow. Soon the Fab Four were at it again, and Benson snapped as good a band shot as youll ever see of as great a band as pop music has ever known. Paul is the key, Benson told the Guardian in 2014. You see how his pillow is up Thats what makes the shot move. The composition reminds me of the famous Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima shot. See page 42. The flag planted by the Beatles would revolutionize popular music

name: The scars of slavery
description: The formerly enslaved man in this photo, known only as Gordon, escaped from his plantation and joined up with a Union Army regiment station in Baton Rouge. When he was examined by the outfits doctors, they saw the scars on his back, the result of whippings he had received, and two photographers who were with the unit asked if they could take Gordons picture. The photo, which became known as The Scourged Back, was printed in Harpers Weekly and was widely circulated by abolitionists who used the image to demonstrate the viciousness of slavery. An unnamed writer in the New York Independent declared its anti slavery message more powerful than Harriet Beecher Stowes book Uncle Toms Cabin because it tells the story in a way that even Mrs. Stowe can not approach, because it tells the story to the eye.

name: A place to protect
description: After breaking up with his fianc e in 1866, Vermont photographer and Civil War veteran William Henry Jackson headed west to escape his troubles, and in 1871 he began to photograph the beauty of the land along the Yellowstone River. His images of natural wonders, including geysers the concept of which sounded fantastical to people who had never seen one, until Jacksons images gave them proof were reproduced and sold around the country, decorating many an American home. His photos helped inspire Congress in 1872 to designate Yellowstone as the countrys first national park, a true landmark moment for Americas conservation movement.

name: Child labor
description: Photographer Lewis Hine could be devious in service to a cause. He presented himself to business owners in a variety of guises, from bible salesman to industrial photographer with an interest in machinery, all for the purpose of gaining entrance to workplaces and documenting the state of child labor in America. Hine took his pictures from 1908 to 1924, at a time when the economy was growing and young people were drawn away from school and into factories. This photo shows breaker boys, whose job it was to pick pieces of slate from conveyor belts as newly broken coal rolled by. Hine was working on behalf of the nonprofit National Childhood Labor Committee, and his pictures were instrumental in generating support for stricter child labor laws

name: Face of the depression
description: Dorothea Lange began her career running a successful portrait studio in San Francisco. After the Great Depression hit, she turned to documentary photography and made a portrait that summed up that difficult age. Lange was among the photogra phers hired by the Farm Security Administration to document the ravages of the Depression, and while shooting pea pickers at a Northern California farm, she came upon this widow and her three children. She said they had been living on frozen vegetables from the surrounding fields and birds the children had killed, Lange recalled years later, after the photo, known as Migrant Mother, had become a symbol of hard times. The photo had such enduring power over the years that the mother, Florence Owens Thompson, and her children came to resent it. Thompson said in an interview, Im tired of symbolizing human poverty when my living conditions have improved.

name: Seeing life
description: The first cover story of the first issue ever of LIFE was about the construction of Fort Peck Dam in Montana, as photographed by the legendary Margaret Bourke White. This picture was accompanied with a caption informing readers that One fourth of the Missouri River will run through this steel liner. LIFE was the first magazine to rely on photos as its primary storytelling medium, and in an internal planning document, founder Henry Luce declared that its mission would be To see life; to see the world; to eyewitness great events to see, and to be shown, is now the will and new expectancy of half mankind. As the success of the magazine showed, his vision about Americas thirst for pictures was spot on

name: American gothic revisited
description: Gordon Parks was working as a photographer for the Farm Security Administration in 1942 when, after a tough day at work in which he was dizzied by the bigotry he encountered, he began talking to a charwoman named Ella Watson. She told me about how her father had been lynched. How her daughter died at childbirth. How she was bringing up two kids on a salary fit for half a person, Parks recalled in the book The Great LIFE Photographers. Parks, who in 1948 became LIFEs first Black staff photographer, called this portrait of Watson in a pose echoing painter Grant Woods American Gothic his first professional photograph, and the one that helped him realize he could use his camera to protest the cruelty of Americas racial divide.

name: The dead sea scrolls
description: In 1947, a young Bedouin shepherd followed a goat into a cave in a cliff north of Israels Dead Sea and came out with a revelatory discovery scrolls in clay jars that, after study and verification, were declared early versions of the books that make up the Hebrew bible. The scrolls, dating from between the third century B. C. to the year 68 A. D., were 1, 000 years older than previously known remnants of early bibles. Further excavation eventually turned up approximately 950 full or partial manu scripts whose contents touched on nearly every book in the Hebrew bible, including some that didnt make it into the version we know today. In their early decades the scrolls remained the province of scholars, but photos meant the Judeo Christian world could feast its eyes on the most historic book release of the century

name: The pinup
description: Betty Grable acted in dozens of movies, but she would quip, I became a star for two reasons, and Im standing on them. Her legs were certainly highlighted in the pinups most famous photo, taken by 20th Century Fox studio photographer Frank Powonly. I asked Betty if shed like to have a back shot, just to be different, Powolny said in a 1982 interview with the Los Angeles Times. She said, Yes, and began to clown around I made only two shots of that pose. It was the second shot that became famous. The photo became the preferred distraction for soldiers during World War II, with five million prints made. The ancients had statues of Aphrodite. The pinup and its progeny were the sculptures photographic heirs

name: Gandhi at his wheel
description: Mohandas Gandhi and the members of his ashram liked to spin fiber into thread for an hour a day, and considered it a holy act. In Margaret Bourke Whites notes on her photograph of the leader who helped force Indias separation from British rule, she wrote, Spinning is raised to the heights almost of a religion with Gandhi and his followers. The spinning wheel is sort of an Ikon to them. Spinning is a cure all and is spoken of in terms of the highest poetry. LIFE ran this photo for the first time in 1946, and again after Gandhis assassination on January 30, 1948. The picture became a representation of a political force who didnt sit high on a throne or command a military but moved millions through his example of nonviolence

name: Career girl
description: If Rosie the Riveter was the face of the American woman during World War II, the Career Girl was her competent postwar successor the secretary, salesclerk, copy writer, or bookkeeper who showed her moxie by striking out on her own and establishing economic independence. In 1948, LIFE exemplified this new archetype in its profile of 23 year old Gwyned Filling, who moved to New York from St. Charles, Missouri, and landed a job in advertising. In the photos and story she emerged as intelligent, hopeful, lonely, and ambitious. Some readers were outraged by Fillings unladylike pursuits, but others applauded the portrayal of a serious young woman.
